_comment: HAND-TRANSCRIBED from CEEDC's published report. No pipeline can regenerate this,
so it is committed on main (districtenergy/raw/ holds the source PDF, gitignored).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL, given we also parse CEEDC's public workbook:
the public download does NOT reproduce the report's totals. CEEDC withheld some
respondent-confidential values from the public file, so every total derived from
the workbook comes out LOWER, on a SMALLER n, than the published analysis. Both
sets are true; they answer different questions. The page must therefore label
report figures as report figures and file figures as file figures, and must never
silently mix them. district_energy_etl.py emits the file-derived side separately
and records the delta in meta.json so the gap is visible rather than papered over.
Source: Griffin, B. (2023). 'District Energy in Canada'. Canadian Energy and
Emissions Data Centre (CEEDC), Simon Fraser University, prepared for

source.title: District Energy in Canada
source.author: Bradford Griffin
source.publisher: Canadian Energy and Emissions Data Centre (CEEDC), Simon Fraser University

survey.distribution: Excel questionnaire, pre-populated with existing data, emailed Spring 2023; reminders and follow-up calls through summer and autumn 2023.
survey.validation: All responses reviewed for errors and substantive omissions; logical inconsistencies (e.g. energy supplied exceeding stated plant capacity) resolved by contacting respondents. Many such problems were incorrect unit conversions.
survey.heterogeneity_caveat: Values were collected over many years. The database records the year each facility's data is reported for, and the source used. Values in the analysis may come from different years or different collection methods.

headline.share_of_building_thermal_energy_basis: Total space heating, space cooling and water heating for apartment, commercial and institutional buildings, NRCan CEUD 2023.
headline.share_of_building_thermal_energy_caveat: Understates district energy: excludes non-respondents and respondents who did not estimate energy supplied.
headline.household_equivalent_basis: NRCan CEUD average residential unit 1,579 ft2 (146.7 m2).
headline.installed_capacity_note: Over one-third (2,530 MW, 42%) of thermal capacity comes from just nine plants providing steam and one providing hot water.
headline.estimated_investment: With ~5,000 MW installed thermal capacity and over 1,000,000 ft of distribution pipe, at roughly $200/kW for boiler plant and ~$1,000/ft for thermal network piping, replacement cost runs to several billion dollars.

systems_by_service._note: Report Table 1. n = 157 systems with a service combination recorded.

rows.service: CHP facility combined with heating and/or cooling

systems_by_service_type._note: Report Figure 3. Systems offer more than one service, so these sum to more than the total. n = 160 with at least one service provided; 78 systems in the database have no service type reported at all.

capacity_by_type._note: Report Table 6. In the 2019 edition capacity values were larger for all energy types despite fewer systems reported; two systems had substantive errors in their capacity values, corrected here.

generation_by_type._note: Report Table 7. n = 119. About 1.4 million MWh of the thermal total is estimated from stated capacity and average capacity factors rather than reported directly.

fuels._note: Report Table 8. Shares sum to more than 100% because a multi-energy system uses several types by definition. n = 238.
fuels.summary: Natural gas is used by over 68% of systems. Over 80% use at least one fossil fuel; 37% use at least one renewable source (biomass, geoexchange or solar thermal). Most CHP systems use natural gas (70%) and/or oil (38%).

energy_and_ghg._note: Report Table 9. Only a limited number of systems reported energy sources. n = 66.

customers._note: Report Table 3. An individual system may serve multiple customer types, so these sum to more than the total. n = 168. Most systems (54%) serve only one customer type.

rows.customer: Commercial (retail, data centre, office, greenhouse, hotel)
Government — First Nation, airport, ministry bldg

investors._note: Report Table 2. Multiple investors may jointly own a system, so shares sum to more than 100%. n = 238.

rows.investor: Federal Government — Other (First Nation, airport, ministry bldg)

investors.summary: Most systems received at least some funding from government (senior 39%, local or municipal 18%) and educational institutions (27%). Private entities including utilities provided 20%.

municipality_size.caveat: Only the large and rural counts are stated numerically in the report; medium and small are shown as bars without labels, so they are left null here rather than read off a chart.

system_age._note: Report Figure 12. n = 174 systems with a commissioning year.

first_system.note: Canada's first district energy system, distributing heat to neighbouring government, university and hospital facilities.

system_age.summary: Over half of all systems were commissioned since 2000; one quarter in the past decade. Another peak construction period runs 1940–1980, with 25% (44) of systems commissioned then. Older systems tend to be the largest; newer systems are likely smaller.
spikes: 1970s oil crisis — a legacy of infrastructure still in operation today.
Late 1990s / early 2000s onward — technological improvement and government support.
system_age.renewables_trend: Since 2000, at least half of all new district energy systems have included some form of renewable energy in their fuel mix, most commonly solid biomass or geothermal heat. n = 169.

physical._note: Report Table 4. Totals across all systems reporting each field.

operating_detail._note: Report Appendix Tables A1–A4. Implied capacity factor = energy supplied ÷ (capacity × 8760 h).

capacity_factors._note: Report section 'Capacity Factors'. Unrealistic values excluded from the average, maximum and minimum.
explanation: Heating and especially cooling seasons are short relative to the whole year.
Most systems carry redundancy — they may run at about half capacity, the rest reserved for peak load and backup.
Systems may plan to expand and add customers.
Old capital is often left in place as additional backup when new capital is installed.
capacity_factors.worked_example: If the heating season is roughly half the year and the system does not supply domestic hot water, utilisation falls to 50%. Running at half of peak output on average takes it to 25%. A full backup halves it again to 12.5%. Keep the replaced boiler as well, and stated utilisation can sit below 10%.

peak_load._note: Asked for the first time in the 2023 edition; not all operators responded.
peak_load.interpretation: The heating range likely reflects operators' willingness or ability to hold backup capacity against mechanical or maintenance outages. Cooling peaks sit closer to installed capacity.

metering._note: Report Figure 20. Share among systems that answered Yes or No.

employment._note: Report Figures 6–9. n = 88 systems reporting full-time equivalent positions.
employment.summary: Hot water systems require fewer employees than steam systems, since provincial boiler and pressure vessel regulations usually require greater supervision. Systems consuming fossil fuels tend to employ more people than systems using renewable energy, and most systems with more than 10 employees are fossil-fuel based. Technical staff make up roughly 80–90% of FTEs (n = 13 for the staffing split).

expansion._note: Report Table 5. Recent expansions in the past five years, among systems that responded.
expansion.summary: Most expansion is in hot water heating. For hot water systems roughly 7% of current buildings were added in the past five years, mostly new building connections, and about 10% of current trench length was added recently.

decarbonization_options._note: Report Table 10. Options being considered in the next five years. n = 27 systems; about 70% of respondents answered this question.
decarbonization_options.summary: Electrification leads: heat pumps (67%) and electric boilers (44%). Industrial heat pumps in particular are maturing quickly. Heat recovery was named by a majority of respondents.

regional._note: Regions are aggregated in the report to maintain respondent confidentiality, so several figures exist only at region level, not province level.
regional.systems: 63 systems in Ontario (26%) and 51 in British Columbia (21%) — together almost half of all systems in Canada.
regional.capacity: Ontario has the highest heating capacity (1,880 MW) and cooling capacity (640 MW). Alberta's capacity is higher than its system count suggests — a smaller number of larger systems.
regional.floor_space: Ontario serves the largest floor area at almost 150 million ft2. British Columbia has added the most systems since 2000 and serves 122 million ft2 — an increase of more than 250% for the 10 largest B.C. systems since the 2019 report.
regional.energy: Ontario uses half the Canadian total (13.2 PJ, 52%), Alberta 4.3 PJ (17%), British Columbia 2.9 PJ (11%). In ON, AB, SK and MB natural gas provides almost all the energy; B.C. is more varied but natural gas still accounts for over 80%.
regional.age: Most construction has been in British Columbia and Ontario, together 49% of systems. The Territories, which had one system built before 1980, have seen three-quarters of their systems constructed since 2000.

conclusions_open_questions: What are the economic costs and benefits of district energy?
Are there key situations where district energy does or does not make sense?
How much energy is saved by the development of district energy?
How can district energy play a stronger role in greenhouse gas mitigation?
limitations_stated_by_ceedc: The currently available survey data are insufficient to conduct a concrete analysis of the energy and GHG savings attributable to district energy.
Heating and cooling energy supplied is difficult to estimate at provincial or national aggregate level, so comparisons to individual systems are inappropriate.

Many systems in the database have energy per unit floor space (GJ/ft2) greater than provincial averages, indicating other factors may matter more when deciding whether to install or connect to a district energy system.

It is unclear whether large efficiency gains are available from district energy, or whether the main benefits relate more to flexibility, reliability and economies of scale in fuel choice (e.g. geoexchange systems that would not be cost effective at individual building scale).
